report:
## Conclusion

**Yes.** Multiple large randomized controlled trials and expert guidelines confirm that regular low-dose CT (LDCT) screening reduces lung cancer death in heavy current and former smokers.

### Key Evidence

1. **National Lung Screening Trial (NLST)** — This U.S. trial randomized 53,454 current or former heavy smokers (ages 55–74) to annual LDCT versus chest X-ray. LDCT screening was associated with a **20% relative reduction in lung cancer mortality**.
   - Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1102873

2. **NELSON Trial (Dutch-Belgian)** — The second-largest RCT, comparing volume-based LDCT screening to no screening in male and female current/former smokers. It found a **24% mortality reduction in men and 33% in women** compared to the unscreened control group, confirming and extending the NLST findings.
   - Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793
   - Commentary: https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanres/article/PIIS2213-2600(20)30059-X/fulltext

3. **USPSTF Recommendation** — Based on this evidence, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends **annual LDCT screening** for adults aged 50–80 with at least a 20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years, concluding with "moderate certainty" that screening has a "moderate net benefit" in this high-risk group.
   - Source: https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening

### Summary

Heavy (ex-)smokers who undergo regular LDCT screening are significantly less likely to die of lung cancer—mortality reductions of roughly 20–26% (and up to 33% in women in NELSON) have been demonstrated. Screening detects cancers at earlier, more treatable stages. The benefit applies specifically to high-risk individuals meeting the smoking-history and age criteria above.
